Chapter 3. Learning From Mistakes and Facing Failure
Let’s be honest—nobody starts out in surgical training expecting to nail everything on the first try. But when failure actually happens, it can still feel like a punch to the gut. That first big mistake? It doesn’t just sting—it feels permanent, almost like you’ve left a mark you can’t erase. And for a lot of residents, there’s this constant, quiet fear: what if I make a mistake that really hurts someone?
Picture this. It’s late, and a resident gets called in for a tough emergency—a bowel obstruction. The pressure is sky-high. In the chaos, something crucial slips through the cracks. Afterward, when the dust settles, it’s clear—a critical step was missed, and now there’s a serious complication. The attending’s disappointment hangs in the air, heavy and unspoken. The resident is left to wrestle with guilt, second-guessing every move. The patient pulls through, thankfully—but the lesson burns deep: every single decision matters, and there’s no escaping responsibility in this line of work.
Here’s something no one really tells you—the culture of medicine can be pretty unforgiving. You’re expected to pick things up fast, adapt on the fly, and never make the same mistake twice. But let’s face it, that’s easier said than done. Even those who seem the most confident can get knocked down by a string of small errors. I remember a colleague, always so steady, suddenly shaken after a rough week. But you know what? Those setbacks made him more careful, more aware. It’s proof—failure, as tough as it is, has a way of teaching lessons you never forget.
There are days when the responsibility feels almost crushing. Imagine finishing a marathon shift, barely able to think straight, and you forget to check a lab result. The result? A patient’s treatment gets delayed, and things take a turn for the worse. The attending doesn’t sugarcoat it—they address the mistake head-on, but there’s no anger, just a clear message: own up, learn from it, and keep moving forward.
That’s when the support of your peers really matters. After a tough case, there’s something comforting about gathering in a quiet corner or over a late-night meal, sharing stories and frustrations. It’s a relief to hear that others have stumbled too—that nobody’s immune to failure. Those honest conversations help lift the weight a little.
Over time, the fear of failing starts to fade. You realize that mistakes are going to happen—and that’s okay. They don’t define who you are. What really counts is your willingness to learn, to ask for help, and to keep pushing yourself to get better. The best surgeons aren’t the ones who never mess up—they’re the ones who turn their failures into stepping stones, becoming more skilled and more compassionate along the way.
It’s a humbling process. It strips away any arrogance and leaves behind a quieter kind of confidence—the kind that comes from facing mistakes, not running from them. In the end, it’s not about chasing perfection. It’s about becoming someone others can trust, especially when the stakes are highest.
